mercy_translation.text:
It seemed good to the Savior to do all these things, so that since human beings had failed to recognize his providence throughout the universe and had not perceived his divinity through creation, they might at least lift their eyes through the works he performed in the body and, through him, receive knowledge of the Father—reasoning, as I said before, from these particular works to his providence over all things.

For who, seeing his authority over demons, or hearing the demons themselves confess him to be their Lord, could still keep his mind in doubt as to whether he is the Son of God, the Wisdom and the Power?

Nor did he allow creation itself to remain silent. Most wonderfully, even at his death—or rather, at his trophy over death, namely the cross—the whole creation confessed that the One made known in the body and suffering there was not merely a human being but the Son of God and Savior of all. The sun turned away, the earth shook, the mountains were split, and all were struck with fear. These things showed Christ upon the cross to be God, while all creation was shown to be his servant and to bear witness through its fear to the presence of its Master.

In this way God the Word manifested himself to human beings through his works. It follows that we should now recount the end of his bodily life and activity and say what kind of death the body underwent—especially since this is the central point of our faith and all people speak continually about it—so that you may know that from this also, no less than from the rest, Christ is known to be God and the Son of God.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius reads the cosmic signs at the crucifixion as creation's testimony to the identity of Christ.
The chapter transitions from the works of Christ to a sustained theological interpretation of his death.
